title: Cooperative Graceful Degradation in Containerized Clouds
problem: Cloud operators lack a mechanism to automatically perform graceful degradation of applications during failures or capacity crunch while simultaneously satisfying application availability requirements and operator infrastructure objectives.
method: Phoenix uses criticality tags on containers to distinguish critical from non-critical services, then applies diagonal scaling—turning off non-critical containers during capacity crunch to free resources for critical services. A Kubernetes-atop controller implements this cooperative graceful degradation by jointly optimizing for both application-defined criticality constraints and operator-level infrastructure objectives. Phoenix handles failures in a cluster of 100,000 nodes within 10 seconds.

title: Reinforcement Learning-Guided Graph State Generation in Photonic Quantum Computers
problem: In photonic quantum computers (PQCs), generating graph states (entangled photon collections) requires finding an optimal generation sequence over quantum emitters, where three fidelity-critical metrics — generation time, number of emitters used, and number of CZ gates — are jointly minimized. Existing compilation frameworks either face exponential search complexity or fail to guarantee optimal results due to their non-deterministic properties.
method: RLGS (Reinforcement Learning-guided Graph State generation) frames the generation sequence problem as an RL optimization task. A map-based abstraction extracts and aligns two-qubit gate dependencies from quantum circuits into a structured representation, enabling the RL agent to detect dependency patterns and search for generation sequences that simultaneously reduce generation time, emitter count, and CZ gate insertions. The framework balances gate serialization depth against crosstalk reduction.

title: From Optimal to Practical: Efficient Micro-op Cache Replacement Policies for Data Center Applications
problem: Data center applications suffer frequent micro-op (uop) cache misses because no effective uop-cache-specific replacement policy exists; the uop cache has fundamentally different cost characteristics from conventional caches (variable and disproportional miss costs, partial hits), making standard policies like LRU and even Belady's algorithm suboptimal.
method: FLACK is introduced as a near-optimal offline replacement policy that accounts for uop cache-specific properties: variable miss costs (due to disproportional re-fetch penalties) and partial hits (when only some micro-ops of an instruction group are cached). FLACK substantially outperforms Belady's algorithm, establishing a new uop-cache-specific optimality bound. FURBYS is then designed as a practical online policy that mimics FLACK via profile-guided methods, using three components: (1) whole-execution hit/miss profiles per static instruction, (2) detection of locally/transiently hot data, and (3) selective ignorance of entries with profiled low hit rates during replacement decisions.

title: A Novel Covert Timing Channel for Cloud FPGAs
problem: Cloud FPGA users face covert data exfiltration risk via side-channel attacks that minimize detection by both victims and cloud providers.
method: Exploits AXI protocol handshake signals and Internet interpacket delay to establish covert timing channel from cloud FPGA to external attacker. Uses timing modulation of AXI handshakes (backpressure, valid/ready) to encode exfiltrated data into network packet timing. Minimal traffic signature avoids cloud provider detection.

title: SDISC: A Spike-Driven Human-Machine Interface with In-Situ Computing for Real-Time Low-Power Interaction
problem: Bio-signal processing for HMI (EMG, EEG) incurs high latency and power using conventional hardware; frame-based methods cannot achieve real-time energy-efficient edge inference.
method: SDISC combines: (1) spike-driven feature extraction (>10x sparsity vs frame-based), (2) RRAM-based in-situ SNN computation (4.09 TOPS/W), (3) Spike-Activity-Distillation and Aid-Loser-Only recovery schemes to handle RRAM non-ideality and long-term drift.

title: Late Breaking Results: Fine-Tuning LLMs for Test Stimuli Generation
problem: LLMs fine-tuned for hardware test stimuli generation often produce inconsistent or incorrect outputs; existing prompt engineering and feedback mechanisms do not effectively improve domain-specific performance in test generation.
method: Two-stage fine-tuning framework: first generates a table-shaped test stimuli dataset to ensure LLM output consistency, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to provide corrective feedback on generated outputs. The approach trains LLMs on domain-specific data with RL signals tuned for test coverage and correctness.

title: YOCO: A Hybrid In-Memory Computing Architecture with 8-bit Sub-PetaOps/W In-Situ Multiply Arithmetic for Large-Scale AI
problem: Analog in-memory computing (AiMC) requires efficient 8-bit multiply operations for AI accelerators with high energy efficiency and throughput.
method: YOCO proposes in-situ multiply arithmetic (IMA) using charge-domain computation and time-domain accumulation, combined with hybrid ReRAM-SRAM memory to balance efficiency and density. An IMC-friendly attention pipeline accelerates transformer inference.

title: DBC: Drift-aware Binary Code for Drift-tolerant Deep Neural Networks
problem: Phase change memory (PCM) cells with multi-level (MLC) operation suffer from conductance drift over time, causing significant accuracy degradation in DNNs stored in PCM.
method: Proposes Drift-aware Binary Code (DBC), a novel binary encoding that maps smaller decimal values to less error-prone PCM cell levels and ensures values shift toward smaller magnitudes upon drift. This maintains DNN accuracy over extended periods because dominant weights are stored at drift-resistant levels, and DNNs tolerate weight decreases better than increases. DBC requires no additional hardware overhead and combines with ECC.

title: EPIC: Error PredIction and Correction for Power-Efficient Voltage Underscaling Multiply-Accumulate Unit
problem: Voltage underscaling enables power savings in MAC units but induces timing errors potentially causing catastrophic accuracy loss in compute-intensive workloads; error correction without high overhead is challenging.
method: EPIC predicts timing errors in underscaled MACs using a prediction bits searching algorithm that maximizes accuracy with low hardware cost, then samples correct output using a delay-tunable clock to correct errors before computational use; achieves up to 100% error correction while maintaining full accuracy.

title: EVA: An Efficient and Versatile Generative Engine for Targeted Discovery of Novel Analog Circuits
problem: Discovering entirely new, high-performance analog circuit topologies is an underexplored challenge; current AI methods focus on topology synthesis from known structures rather than generative discovery of novel designs.
method: EVA uses a decoder-only transformer with bottom-up generation to sequentially predict device pin connections and create circuits from scratch. Pretraining on unlabeled circuit topologies builds connectivity knowledge; fine-tuning via PPO and DPO optimizes for high-performance designs.

title: Efficient and Scalable Architectures for Multi-level Superconducting Qubit Readout
problem: Superconducting transmons are multi-level systems where leakage into energy levels outside the computational subspace complicates quantum error correction (QEC). Detecting and mitigating leakage requires effective multi-level readout, but current approaches consume excessive FPGA resources and readout time.
method: Scalable three-level readout architecture using matched filters to detect relaxation and excitation error patterns, combined with a modular lightweight neural network to correct crosstalk errors. Implements bit-serial detection and integrates into off-the-shelf FPGA.

title: Systematic CXL Memory Characterization and Performance Analysis at Scale
problem: CXL-attached memory introduces sub-microsecond latency overheads (140-410 ns) relative to local DRAM, but the performance impact across diverse devices, CPU platforms, and workloads is poorly understood, including tail latencies, prefetcher behavior, and bottleneck localization.
method: Melody is a characterization framework that runs 265 workloads across 4 real CXL devices, 5 CPU platforms, and 7 injected latency levels to comprehensively profile CXL memory performance. It introduces SPA (Sub-operation Performance Analysis), a novel methodology that decomposes memory access latency into sub-operations to pinpoint CXL-specific bottlenecks. Melody also measures and discloses CXL tail latency distributions for the first time, and characterizes CPU hardware prefetcher effectiveness (and failures) under CXL latency conditions.

title: Nyx: Virtualizing dataflow execution on shared FPGA platforms
problem: Existing multi-tenant FPGA virtualization systems support only task-parallel models, where distinct reconfigurable regions process independent data batches — this precludes dataflow execution (direct streaming between pipelined tasks), forcing dependent tasks to wait and incurring long end-to-end response times. No prior work supports dataflow pipelines in a virtualized, shared FPGA environment.
method: Nyx partitions the FPGA into distinct partially-reconfigurable regions and introduces virtual FIFOs — independent communication channels that decouple pipelined tasks from their predecessors and successors. When a task occupies one region, virtual FIFOs buffer inter-task data so that dependent tasks need not be co-scheduled simultaneously on the fabric. An FPGA hypervisor manages all data dependencies, tracks FIFO state, and dispatches pipelined tasks across regions at high throughput, enabling temporal multiplexing of dataflow pipelines across shared hardware.

title: 3D-SubG: A 3D Stacked Hybrid Processing Near/In-Memory Accelerator for Subgraph GNNs
problem: Subgraph Graph Neural Networks have complex irregular structures with numerous independent subgraphs, creating severe bandwidth bottlenecks and poor data reuse in conventional architectures, limiting throughput.
method: 3D stacks logic die with DRAM die via hybrid bonding; logic die employs SRAM-based processing-in-memory macros for computation density; bit-level non-zero gathering exploits graph sparsity; workload-balanced mapping allocates subgraphs to logic-DRAM blocks; distributed global pooling reduces inter-block data movements.

title: Protecting Cryptographic Code Against Spectre-RSB: (and, in Fact, All Known Spectre Variants)
problem: Constant-time cryptographic code is designed to prevent timing-based secret leakage, but Spectre attacks—especially Spectre-RSB (Return Stack Buffer)—can violate constant-time guarantees by leaking secrets during speculative execution, and prior defenses cover only Spectre-v1 while leaving other Spectre variants unaddressed.
method: The approach combines a new value-dependent information-flow type system with a compiler transformation. The type system statically tracks whether values depend on secrets and whether they may flow to speculative-execution leak channels (cache, port contention, etc.) under any of the known Spectre mistraining variants. The compiler transformation rewrites low-level code to enforce the type-system restrictions—inserting fences, reordering, and masking as needed—so that no secret-dependent value reaches a speculative leak channel. Both the type-system soundness and the correctness of the compiler transformation are machine-proved in the Coq proof assistant, then implemented in the Jasmin high-assurance cryptography framework.

title: Cinnamon: A Framework for Scale-Out Encrypted AI
problem: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) imposes orders-of-magnitude performance overhead for ML inference, and prior FHE accelerators use massive monolithic chip designs that do not scale to large models like BERT and provide poor performance-per-dollar.
method: Cinnamon is a scale-out FHE acceleration framework that exploits parallelism at all program levels using novel algorithms, a compiler, and a chiplet-based hardware design. The compiler identifies and schedules FHE operation parallelism (polynomial NTT, RNS decomposition, key-switching) across multiple chips, while architectural extensions reduce per-chip resource requirements to enable economical scaling. Novel algorithms reduce communication volume between chiplets, enabling a distributed multi-chip FHE accelerator rather than a single monolithic die.
